variants.title: Read the queue pressure
variants.context: Burst ingress = baseline arrival × burst multiplier. Consumer capacity = workers × 1,000 ÷ service time in ms. Backlog grows by max(0, ingress − capacity); when capacity exceeds baseline, drain time = backlog ÷ spare capacity.
variants.prompt: Eight workers each take 250 ms per message. What is the consumer capacity in messages per second?

mistakes.feedback: Divide 1,000 by the service time before multiplying.
That is one worker’s rate; there are eight.

variants.title: Read the queue pressure
variants.context: Burst ingress = baseline arrival × burst multiplier. Consumer capacity = workers × 1,000 ÷ service time in ms. Backlog grows by max(0, ingress − capacity); when capacity exceeds baseline, drain time = backlog ÷ spare capacity.
variants.prompt: A burst brings 100 messages per second for 60 seconds while capacity is 32 per second. How many messages accumulate?
variants.hint: Backlog grows by ingress minus capacity, per second.

mistakes.feedback: Consumers still drain 32 per second during the burst.
Multiply by the 60 seconds of burst.

variants.title: Read the queue pressure
variants.context: Burst ingress = baseline arrival × burst multiplier. Consumer capacity = workers × 1,000 ÷ service time in ms. Backlog grows by max(0, ingress − capacity); when capacity exceeds baseline, drain time = backlog ÷ spare capacity.
variants.prompt: After the burst, baseline arrival returns to 20 per second and capacity is 32 per second. How long does a 4,080-message backlog take to drain?
variants.hint: Drain time = backlog ÷ spare capacity, where spare = capacity − baseline.
variants.explanation: Spare capacity is 32 − 20 = 12 per second. 4,080 ÷ 12 = 340 seconds. Check that against the business deadline.

mistakes.feedback: Baseline traffic keeps arriving; only the spare 12 per second drains the backlog.

variants.title: Time the acknowledgement
variants.context: Acknowledge before processing for at-most-once behavior (a crash loses work). Acknowledge after the durable effect for at-least-once (a lost acknowledgement redelivers). Effectively-once combines at-least-once delivery with a stable ID and an idempotent effect.
variants.prompt: A consumer acknowledges as soon as it receives a message, then crashes mid-processing. What happened to the work?
options: The producer retries it after its own send timeout expires.
It is lost; the broker will not redeliver an acknowledged message.
The broker notices the crash and redelivers the message automatically.
optionFeedback: Producers do not watch consumer crashes; their send already succeeded.
Acknowledge-before-processing is at-most-once behavior.
The acknowledgement already released the broker's copy, so nothing returns.
variants.hint: What does the acknowledgement tell the broker?
variants.explanation: Acknowledge after the durable effect when work must not be lost.

variants.title: Time the acknowledgement
variants.context: Acknowledge before processing for at-most-once behavior (a crash loses work). Acknowledge after the durable effect for at-least-once (a lost acknowledgement redelivers). Effectively-once combines at-least-once delivery with a stable ID and an idempotent effect.
variants.prompt: A consumer commits its effect, then the acknowledgement is lost. What must the consumer tolerate?
options: A redelivery of the same message, made harmless by its stored ID.
Nothing; the broker can see the effect was committed downstream.
A rollback of the committed effect once the ack is found missing.
optionFeedback: At-least-once delivery redelivers; the stored ID makes it harmless.
The broker only knows what was acknowledged; it cannot see your database.
A lost acknowledgement never reaches back into a committed transaction.
variants.hint: From the broker’s view, what does a lost ack look like?
variants.explanation: Store the message ID with the business update in one transaction so redelivery converges.

variants.title: Time the acknowledgement
variants.context: Acknowledge before processing for at-most-once behavior (a crash loses work). Acknowledge after the durable effect for at-least-once (a lost acknowledgement redelivers). Effectively-once combines at-least-once delivery with a stable ID and an idempotent effect.
variants.prompt: What gives an effectively-once business result?
options: At-most-once delivery, so no message is ever processed twice.
A broker setting called exactly-once delivery, enabled on the queue and topic.
At-least-once delivery plus a stable message ID and an idempotent effect.
optionFeedback: At-most-once avoids duplicates by losing work, which is the worse failure.
No broker makes an arbitrary email or card charge happen exactly once.
The broker may repeat delivery while the user observes one result.
variants.hint: Which combination survives both redelivery and loss?
variants.explanation: Correctness crosses the broker boundary only when the consumer and external system share an idempotency contract.

variants.title: Close the uncertainty windows
variants.context: Two uncertainty windows need design: a database write can commit while publication fails, and a consumer effect can commit while acknowledgement fails. Outbox on the producer side; store the message ID with the effect on the consumer side.
variants.prompt: An order confirmation must reach email and fulfillment. Put the recoverable path in order.

items.text: The broker confirms publication only after its durability level is met.
The consumer stores the message ID with its business update in one transaction.
Acknowledge after success; retry transient failures with a deadline; dead-letter permanent ones.
Write the business state and an outbox event in one database transaction.

variants.hint: The acknowledgement is deliberately outside the consumer’s transaction.
variants.explanation: Outbox → durable accept → effect with stored ID → acknowledge or redrive. A lost ack redelivers, but the stored identity prevents a second confirmation.

variants.title: Close the uncertainty windows
variants.context: Two uncertainty windows need design: a database write can commit while publication fails, and a consumer effect can commit while acknowledgement fails. Outbox on the producer side; store the message ID with the effect on the consumer side.
variants.prompt: A relay crashes right after publishing. Put the path that keeps this safe in order.

items.text: It acknowledges; the retry budget and dead-letter policy remain unchanged.
State and outbox event were committed together earlier.
The relay republishes the same event ID after restart; the broker accepts durably.
The consumer sees the ID already recorded and treats the second delivery as a no-op.

variants.hint: Same event ID on republish is what makes the crash harmless.
variants.explanation: A relay can retry publication without inventing a new event ID.

variants.title: Close the uncertainty windows
variants.context: Two uncertainty windows need design: a database write can commit while publication fails, and a consumer effect can commit while acknowledgement fails. Outbox on the producer side; store the message ID with the effect on the consumer side.
variants.prompt: A consumer effect commits, then the process dies before acknowledging. Put the recovery in order.

items.text: The broker makes the unacknowledged message available again after its timeout.
The redelivered message matches a stored message ID, so the effect is not repeated.
The outbox had already made publication durable.

variants.hint: The broker cannot tell a crash from slow work.
variants.explanation: Redelivery after a timeout is expected; the stored message ID is what prevents a duplicate effect.

variants.title: Read the right signal
variants.context: Oldest-message age is usually more actionable than depth. Scale from sustained age and utilization, not a depth threshold. Messages carry a stable ID, entity and partition key, schema version, deadline, and correlation ID.
variants.prompt: Ten thousand thumbnail jobs are queued, and one password-reset message has waited past its deadline. Which is the incident?
options: The password reset: its oldest-message age is past the deadline.
The thumbnails, because ten thousand queued jobs is the bigger number.
Neither, since both queues are below the configured depth threshold.
optionFeedback: Depth means different things for replayable streams, bursty task queues, and five-second user deadlines.
Ten thousand thumbnails with no deadline are backlog, not an incident.
A deadline breach is an incident regardless of depth.
variants.hint: Which metric relates to a business deadline?
variants.explanation: Alert on age and deadline breaches by message type; scale from sustained age and utilization.

variants.title: Read the right signal
variants.context: Oldest-message age is usually more actionable than depth. Scale from sustained age and utilization, not a depth threshold. Messages carry a stable ID, entity and partition key, schema version, deadline, and correlation ID.
variants.prompt: A team autoscales workers from a single depth threshold. What is the better trigger?
options: Sustained oldest-message age and utilization.
A lower depth threshold so scaling starts sooner.
The number of queues the service consumes from.
optionFeedback: Age and utilization describe whether work is progressing toward its deadline.
Depth still ignores deadlines and message types.
Queue count is a topology fact and says nothing about progress.
variants.hint: What does depth fail to tell you?
variants.explanation: Depth has different meanings for different queues; age and utilization are comparable.

variants.title: Read the right signal
variants.context: Oldest-message age is usually more actionable than depth. Scale from sustained age and utilization, not a depth threshold. Messages carry a stable ID, entity and partition key, schema version, deadline, and correlation ID.
variants.prompt: Which fields belong in a message contract?
options: The full database row plus the consumer code version that will read it.
Only the payload fields the consumer needs to do its job.
A stable ID, partition key, schema version, deadline, and a small payload.
optionFeedback: Large payloads and coupling to consumer versions make messages brittle.
Without identity and version, duplicates and schema changes are invisible.
Self-identifying messages can be deduplicated, ordered, versioned, and traced.
variants.hint: What does a consumer need to process safely and explain the outcome?
variants.explanation: Keep messages small and self-identifying; reference large data durably.

variants.title: Pick the ownership model
variants.context: Competing consumers share a backlog; independent subscriptions each keep their own progress; partitioned ordering keeps one key’s events in order; delayed redrive retries with jitter and a bounded attempt count.
variants.prompt: Image processing jobs should be shared across a pool of workers. Which model?
options: Partitioned ordering.
Competing consumers.
Independent subscriptions.
optionFeedback: Ordering is not the requirement.
Each message is owned by one worker at a time; add workers to increase throughput.
Subscriptions deliver every message to every subscriber.
variants.hint: Should each job reach one worker or every worker?
variants.explanation: Competing consumers distribute tasks until a partition, dependency, or hot key limits them.

variants.title: Pick the ownership model
variants.context: Competing consumers share a backlog; independent subscriptions each keep their own progress; partitioned ordering keeps one key’s events in order; delayed redrive retries with jitter and a bounded attempt count.
variants.prompt: Billing, analytics, and search each need every order event and must not block one another. Which model?
options: Independent subscriptions, each with its own progress marker.
Competing consumers reading from one shared order queue.
One consumer that reads the queue and calls the other two services.
optionFeedback: One slow subscriber should not prevent another from advancing.
Competing consumers split the messages, so each service sees only a share.
A single consumer couples the reactions; one slow call blocks the others.
variants.hint: Does each consumer need its own copy?

variants.title: Pick the ownership model
variants.context: Competing consumers share a backlog; independent subscriptions each keep their own progress; partitioned ordering keeps one key’s events in order; delayed redrive retries with jitter and a bounded attempt count.
variants.prompt: One order’s status updates must be applied in order, but different orders can proceed in parallel. Which model?
options: Partitioned ordering keyed by the order.
Global ordering across the whole queue.
Random distribution.
optionFeedback: Related events route to the same partition; more partitions add parallelism without global order.
Global order limits parallelism and enlarges the failure domain.
Random routing discards per-order order.
variants.hint: What is the smallest unit that needs order?
variants.explanation: Partition by the entity whose events require local ordering.
